dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper addresses the bottleneck of extracting a high-dimensional function f, such as a financial pricing function, from a quantum state where its values are encoded in amplitudes, noting that naive readout can be so time‑consuming that any quantum speedup is lost (C-001). The authors seek generally applicable methods for this function-extraction task (C-004), with the practical goal of obtaining an approximation of f that is efficiently computable on a classical computer (C-011). They numerically study this in a finance setting by approximating a worst-of put option price function (C-003, C-035).

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The proposed approach combines orthogonal function expansion with tensor networks to approximate the target function f with a polynomial number of degrees of freedom (C-002). Expansion coefficients are defined via inner products ⟨P_l|f⟩ using a discretely orthogonal basis, which the authors then tensorize for the multivariate case (C-005, C-016, C-017, C-018). To control the exponential growth from naive tensorization (C-006), they represent the coefficient tensor as a matrix product state (MPS) (C-007), using a quantum circuit VMPS that prepares an MPS-encoded coefficient state |ã⟩ (C-009, C-024) whose parameters correspond to the tensor entries (C-022, C-025). The full circuit has two parts: first encoding the MPS coefficients of the orthogonal expansion (C-012, C-013), then applying a fixed unitary that maps these coefficients to a state |f̃̃⟩ whose amplitudes encode the approximate function (C-014). Circuit parameters are optimized via an alternating block procedure to maximize fidelity with the target state (C-010, C-015, C-029, C-030), estimating required matrix elements using the Hadamard test (C-031), and finally outputting a scaled approximation C f̃̃ as the classical proxy for f (C-028, C-032).

dimension_3_key_results.text: Using a classical simulation, the authors demonstrate that their MPS-based orthogonal expansion can approximate a finance-motivated function—the worst-of put price—such that the MPS-based approximation fits Monte Carlo values within about 0.5 absolute error or less (C-003, C-040), and nearly overlaps the full cosine expansion approximation (C-041). They report that the MPS representation achieves a large parameter compression: 12,544 degrees of freedom versus 1,048,576 cosine coefficients, a reduction by about two orders of magnitude (C-042), while maintaining efficient classical evaluation cost O(dr^2 D + r D^2) (C-023). An additional experiment indicates a power-law relationship between approximation accuracy and the number of degrees of freedom in the large-DOF regime (C-043), and that their reduced model outperforms a low-degree cosine expansion with similar DOF (C-044). Overall, the authors interpret these findings as supporting the proposed method in the tested finance setting (C-045).

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: The method is benchmarked against classical Monte Carlo integration and full cosine-basis expansions of the option price function (C-035, C-037). The MPS-based approximation is reported to fit Monte Carlo integration values well within an error of about 0.5 or less (C-040) and to almost overlap the full cosine-expansion approximation despite using far fewer parameters (C-041, C-042). Moreover, for comparable degrees of freedom, a low-degree cosine expansion has much larger error than the proposed MPS-based approximation f̃̃′ (C-044), indicating a favorable comparison in terms of accuracy per parameter.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors acknowledge several limitations. On the algorithmic side, direct amplitude readout of |f⟩ suffers from amplitudes that are exponentially suppressed by a factor 1/N_gr with respect to dimension d, making naive extraction inefficient (C-019). To circumvent this, they rely on expansion coefficients whose ratios are expected to be O(1), but this is an assumption rather than a proven bound (C-020). The MPS circuit parameterization imposes a normalization constraint on the first tensor block due to unitarity (C-026), implying that the overall scale of the approximation f̃̃ cannot be directly adjusted within the circuit (C-027), so an external estimate C for the scale of f relative to f̃̃ is required to form the final approximation C f̃̃ (C-028). They also note that they do not provide an explicit bound on the total query complexity for the oracles Of and V_i^OF, and that deriving such complexity estimates is currently difficult (C-046, C-048). Finally, they state that the convergence properties of the alternating optimization method used to tune circuit blocks are not well understood theoretically (C-047).

dimension_6_future_work.text: The authors highlight two main directions for future work: developing explicit complexity estimates for the overall algorithm, including query complexity for the required oracles, which they state is desired but difficult at present (C-048), and combining their generic function-extraction method with concrete function-finding quantum algorithms on specific application problems (C-049).

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The paper presents a general, hybrid-style procedure to extract an approximate, classically evaluable function from a quantum state by combining orthogonal function expansion with tensor-network (MPS) representations, thereby reducing the number of degrees of freedom from exponential to polynomial under certain conditions (C-002, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-011). They emphasize that a simple quantum circuit can generate a state whose amplitudes encode an MPS-structured orthogonal expansion (C-009, C-013, C-014, C-024), and that an existing general procedure for optimizing tensor-network circuits is adapted here to maximize fidelity with the function-encoding state (C-010, C-015, C-029, C-030, C-031). The approach is claimed to be broadly applicable to function-extraction tasks beyond the initial PDE-motivated context (C-033).

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the work is largely theoretical with classical numerical experiments used as a proxy for quantum execution. The authors clearly specify key modeling and basis assumptions, including discrete orthogonality of the chosen basis functions and their tensorized construction (C-016, C-017, C-036, C-037). They quantify the parameter count of the MPS representation (C-022) and give an explicit scaling for the number of arithmetic operations needed to evaluate the resulting approximation on a classical computer (C-023), aiding reproducibility and complexity assessment. The numerical setup is described with explicit parameter choices such as dimension d, grid size D, bond dimension r, iteration count, and other experimental parameters (C-039), and they report systematic exploration of accuracy versus degrees of freedom and basis degree (C-043, C-044). For the optimization, they describe using an alternating update strategy and, in principle, Hadamard-test-based estimates for matrix elements (C-030, C-031, C-038). They also discuss a classical modification of the fidelity objective (from F to F′ = ⟨a|ã⟩) to make the numerical experiment feasible (C-038), clarifying that the experiments operate on classically computed expansion coefficients rather than on an actual quantum device.

dimension_9_miscellaneous.text: The paper observes that direct amplitude readout is hindered by exponential suppression in high dimensions (C-019), but that working with expansion coefficients can avoid such suppression because relevant amplitude ratios are expected to remain O(1) (C-020). These insights, while tied to the main method, also offer a more general perspective on designing readout schemes for amplitude-encoded functions.
